n: This lecture is devoted to hallucinogens and other controlled substances. The topic: phencyclidine, ketamine, psilocin, psilocybin, LSD and their analysis. According to the outline, we first review the general definition, then phencyclidine and its analogues, ketamine, LSD, psilocin and psilocybin. The analytical part covers isolation, colour reactions, thin-layer chromatography, ultraviolet and infrared spectroscopy and mass spectrometry. Key terms: hallucinogen, phencyclidine, ketamine, LSD, psilocybin, Scott reagent, Ehrlich reagent and van Urk reagent.

The hallucinogen group includes substances of various chemical structures, but they act on the central nervous system in almost the same way. When abused, mood and thinking change, the central nervous system is excited, and euphoria or severe depression arises. As a result of depersonalisation, accidents occur. In other words, although the structures of these substances differ, the general picture of their effect on the body is similar.

By chemical structure, hallucinogens can be assigned to three groups: indole, phencyclidine and amphetamine derivatives. The indole derivatives include lysergic acid diethylamide, that is, LSD, bufotenine, psilocybin and psilocin. The phencyclidine derivatives group contains phencyclidine and its analogues. The amphetamine derivatives group includes DOM, or STP, and mescaline, which are covered in lessons 36-37. The table shows these groups and their representatives.

Now the history of phencyclidine. Chemically, phencyclidine is 1-(1-phenylcyclohexyl)-piperidine. It was synthesised in the 1950s as a drug for anaesthesia. Because it caused many adverse effects in use, it was withdrawn from circulation in 1979. That is, the substance was first made for medicine and then withdrawn because of its adverse effects.

The following signs are observed when phencyclidine is taken. First of all, euphoria, relaxation, detachment from reality, a feeling of lightness in the body and a surge of physical strength are felt. Rapid involuntary eye movement, reduced hearing, loss of balance and inhibition also occur. In addition, blood pressure rises and tachycardia arises.

Physico-chemical properties of phencyclidine. Phencyclidine base is a crystalline substance with a melting point of 46-46.6 °C. Its hydrochloride and hydrobromide salts are also crystalline; their melting points are 243-244 °C and 225-226 °C respectively. As to solubility, its salts dissolve in water, ethanol and chloroform. The base dissolves in ether, chloroform, benzene and other solvents.

Phencyclidine has a stimulating and hallucinogenic effect on the central nervous system. As an analgesic it is taken at a dose of 1-7 mg. The maximum blood concentration appears at 5-15 minutes. When taken by smoking, the maximum appears after 2 hours. Thus the time of onset of the effect differs depending on the route of intake.

t: Routes of intake and forms of phencyclidine
n: Phencyclidine enters the body by several routes: intravenously, by nasal sniffing and by smoking. It is rarely taken by mouth. It occurs as a substance, solution, tablets and capsules. It may also occur impregnated into marijuana, makhorka, parsley or mint leaf. A single dose is produced from 0.001 to 0.007 g.

With overdose, hypertension, tachycardia, loss of consciousness and death occur. The table on the slide gives phencyclidine concentrations in various specimens in mg/l: in blood 4.8, in urine 35, in brain 7.3 and in liver 23. Ranges are also shown in brackets. Remember: in the textbook these values are given in general terms, while in the malaka source the same values are attributed to fatal poisonings, n=17.

Phencyclidine metabolism. Biologically active metabolites are formed by hydroxylation of the piperidine and cyclohexane rings. The main amount, 70%, is excreted by the kidneys as conjugates over 7 hours. At the same time, phencyclidine can persist in blood plasma for up to 10 days.

Isolation of phencyclidine. From biological fluids it is extracted from an alkaline medium with various organic solvents. At pH=9.6 the recovery depends on the solvent: in hexane 58%, in heptane 60%, in toluene 91%, in ethyl acetate 97%, and in heptane-isoamyl alcohol 98%. Solid-phase extraction, that is, isolation on microcolumns, is also used. In addition, it is isolated by the acidified water or alcohol method and then extracted in an alkaline medium.

Preliminary colour reactions of phencyclidine. With Marquis reagent a light pink colour forms, with Mandelin reagent orange. When Ehrlich reagent is added, a red product appears. With Scott reagent, that is, with 1 drop of 16% HCl and 1 drop of 2.5% cobalt thiocyanate, a blue product forms. These reactions are preliminary, that is, presumptive tests.

Phencyclidine and its derivatives are examined by thin-layer chromatography in three systems. The first system: a mixture of ethyl acetate, methanol and ammonia 25%, ratio 85:10:5, on silica gel. The second system: cyclohexane, toluene and diethylamine, ratio 75:15:10; the silica gel is treated with 0.1 mol/l KOH. The third system: chloroform and methanol, ratio 90:10, the silica gel again treated with 0.1 mol/l KOH. The spots are visualised under UV light, with iodoplatinate and with Dragendorff reagent according to Munier.

Rf values of phencyclidine derivatives. For phencyclidine the Rf values in systems 1, 2 and 3 are 0.84, 0.73 and 0.35 respectively. For tenocyclidine 0.86, 0.73 and 0.54. For eticyclidine 0.79, 0.65 and 0.27. For rolicyclidine 0.79, 0.66 and 0.25. In the table all four substances are given side by side, and by comparing these values the substances can be distinguished.

t: Phencyclidine: GLC, GC-MS and quantitative analysis
n: As visualising reagents, UV light, potassium iodoplatinate solution and Dragendorff reagent modified according to Munier are used. Then the substance is identified by GLC from retention time, using a flame ionisation detector. In GC-MS, peaks at 243, 214, 200, 186, 166, 158, 84 and 77 m/z are formed. The amount is determined by GLC or HPLC.

Ketamine, otherwise Calypsol, is a synthetic psychotropic substance with a hypnotic effect; the effect lasts 2 hours. In the pharmaceutical industry it is produced as powder and solution in ampoules and vials. At high doses it causes hallucinations. It also produces high tolerance, that is, the dose must be increased to obtain the effect.

Isolation of ketamine. From a biological specimen and blood it is isolated by soaking, using water acidified with sulphuric acid. From the aqueous extract it is extracted with chloroform in an alkaline medium, at pH=8-9. The procedure in urine is as follows: 50 ml of urine is brought to pH 8-9 with 25% ammonia, then extracted 3 times with 15 ml of chloroform, and the volume is made up to 50 ml.

The reaction of ketamine with copper sulphate. 5 drops of the chloroform solution are placed in a test tube, and after the solvent evaporates, 0.5 ml of 0.1 M HCl is added to the residue. Then 1 drop of 10% copper sulphate, 1 ml of 10% sodium hydroxide and 1 ml of diethyl ether are added and mixed. As a result the ether layer turns pink-violet.

t: Ketamine: sodium nitrite and naphthol reaction
n: The reaction of ketamine with sodium nitrite and naphthol. The organic solvent is evaporated from the chloroform solution, 3 ml of conc. sulphuric acid and 0.4 g of sodium nitrite are added to the residue, and it is heated on a water bath for 10 minutes. A small amount of zinc dust is added and filtered. To the filtrate, 2-3 drops each of 2% sodium nitrite and alkaline naphthol solutions are added. The mixture turns red-cherry. If ketamine is present in a small amount, light pink is seen, then brown-violet, then yellow-green.

The reaction with Nessler reagent is microcrystalloscopic. On a slide, 1-2 drops of chloroform solution are evaporated, and 1 drop of Nessler reagent is dropped on the residue. Under the microscope, colourless clustered needle-shaped microcrystals are seen. In thin-layer chromatography, on a silica gel-G (Merck) plate, an orange-brown spot forms with iodoplatinate and a dark blue spot with iodine vapour.

Ketamine is examined by thin-layer chromatography in several systems. TA: methanol-ammonia 25%, ratio 100:1.5. TB: cyclohexane-toluene-diethylamine, 75:15:10. TC: chloroform-methanol, 90:10. TE: ethyl acetate-methanol-ammonia, 85:10:5. TAE: methanol. TAL: chloroform-methanol-propionic acid, 72:18:10. Rf values: in TA and TB 0.59 and 0.73; in TC and TE 0.35 and 0.84; in TAE and TAL 0.23 and 0.48.

Ketamine is also determined by GLC and HPLC. For GLC: glass column 2 m x 2 mm, phase 3% SE-30 on Chromosorb G-HP; carrier nitrogen 45 ml/min; temperature varies from 100 to 300 °C. The retention index of ketamine is RI 1840. In HPLC a C18 column (250 x 4.6 mm, 5 µm) is used, 40 °C, mobile phase water-acetonitrile-2.5 M H2SO4, ratio 50:50:0.1; a diode-array UV detector is used. The retention time is 4.18.

t: Ketamine: UV, IR and mass spectra
n: Spectral features of ketamine. A solution in 0.1 M HCl absorbs maximally at 269 and 276 nm. In the infrared spectrum, in KBr, absorption bands are observed at 1696, 747, 1142, 1120, 712 and 1027 cm-1. In the mass spectrum, peaks at 180, 209, 182, 152, 181, 30, 211 and 138 m/z are formed. Together, these three data serve to confirm ketamine.

Hallucinogens also include lysergic acid diethylamide, bufotenine, psilocybin, psilocin and others. LSD was first synthesised in 1938 in the Swiss “Sandoz” laboratory by Dr A. Hofmann. LSD is a semi-synthetic substance obtained from the alkaloids of ergot, Secale cornutum, ascomycete fungi of the Claviceps family.

t: Action of LSD on the body
n: Action of LSD on the body. LSD is rapidly absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract and reaches all organs and tissues. When taken orally at a dose of 2 µg/kg, the maximum concentration appears at 30-60 minutes. The duration of action is 8-12 hours. The minimum dose causing hallucinations is 10-25 µg.

When LSD is taken, the pupil dilates, blood pressure rises, body temperature increases, and sweating, nausea and tremor are observed; then psychic agitation, paranoia and psychosis develop. Complications: chromosomal damage, birth of disabled children; suicide is also possible. LSD is a colourless, odourless crystalline powder. It does not dissolve in water, dissolves well in organic solvents and has the properties of a base.

When LSD is heated in 7% alkali solution for 1 hour, it is hydrolysed to lysergic acid and diethylamine. 1% of LSD is excreted from the body unchanged in urine. The rest undergoes dealkylation and oxidation and is excreted as glucuronides. Consequently, the share of unchanged substance in urine is very small.

Isolation of LSD. Blood and urine are taken for analysis; LSD and its metabolites are isolated by solid-phase extraction. It is advisable to analyse LSD and its metabolites within 72 hours. From the preparation and biological fluids, LSD is extracted with organic solvents; chlorobutane or a mixture of methylene chloride and toluene is used.

Colour reactions of LSD. With Marquis reagent, LSD forms a colour turning from orange-brown to violet. With p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde, conc. H2SO4 and iron (III) chloride, that is, van Urk reagent, a red-violet or violet colour appears. Remember: the van Urk reaction is common to ergot alkaloids. With conc. H2SO4 and Froehde reagent the specificity of the reaction is low.

Detection of LSD by thin-layer chromatography. The plate used is “Silufol UV-254”. Visualising reagent: first UV light, 366 nm, then Ehrlich reagent. Systems: chloroform-acetone-ethanol-ammonia 25%, ratio 20:20:3:1; ethyl acetate-isopropanol-ammonia, 5:5:1; hexane-acetone-ammonia, 2:2:0.2. For LSD Rf=0.57.

Ultraviolet spectrophotometry of LSD. A solution in 0.1 M hydrochloric acid gives a maximum at 315 nm, and a solution in 0.1 M sodium hydroxide at 310 nm. The spectrum of LSD eluted from the thin-layer plate, in a methanol-water-HCl mixture, ratio 50:50:1, is seen at 249, 317 and 200 nm. In a toluene-acetone-ethanol-ammonia mixture, 45:45:7:3, maxima are observed at 243 and 315 nm.

t: LSD: IR, GC-MS and quantitative analysis
n: The infrared spectrum of LSD, in KBr, gives absorption at 1626, 1307, 1136, 1066, 1212 and 749 cm-1. In GC-MS, peaks at 44, 72, 207, 221, 280 and 323 m/z are observed. The amount is determined by UV spectrophotometry, GC-MS and HPLC. In addition, the coloured product obtained with Ehrlich reagent is also measured by the photoelectrocolorimetry (PEC) method.

Psilocin and psilocybin are synthesised on the basis of dimethyltryptamine, that is, DMT; psilocin is a metabolite of psilocybin. They occur in hallucinogenic mushrooms: of the genera Psilocybe, Stropharia, Copelandia, Panaeolina, Panaeolus and others. Psilocybin was isolated from a mushroom in 1958.

The action of psilocin and psilocybin is similar to LSD. Hallucinations begin 30 minutes after intake, and the effect lasts 6 hours. One mushroom contains 1 mg of psilocin and 16 mg of psilocybin. At 4-8 mg of both substances, or about 2 g of dried mushroom, they cause hallucinations, and at 8-20 mg psychic changes.

t: Psilocin and psilocybin: UV and IR
n: Ultraviolet and infrared characteristics of psilocin and psilocybin. The aqueous solution of psilocin at pH<7.0 gives maxima at 266, 283 and 292 nm, at pH>7.0 at 270 and 293 nm. The aqueous solution of psilocybin at pH<7.0 gives a maximum at 268 nm, at pH>7.0 at 269, 282 and 292 nm. In the infrared spectrum, in KBr, psilocin gives values of 836, 1261, 1236, 1042, 1061 and 733 cm-1; psilocybin 1105, 1045, 1062, 1183, 1160 and 932 cm-1.

t: Psilocin and psilocybin: MS and quantity
n: In the mass spectrum of psilocin, peaks at 58, 204, 59, 42, 30, 146, 77 and 44 m/z are observed. In the mass spectrum of psilocybin, peaks at 58, 42, 30, 51, 204, 146, 77 and 44 m/z occur. The amount is determined by UV spectrophotometry and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry.

Comparing the three substances gives the following picture. Phencyclidine was synthesised in the 1950s for anaesthesia and withdrawn from circulation in 1979; it has a stimulating and hallucinogenic effect. Ketamine is a synthetic psychotropic substance whose hypnotic effect lasts 2 hours, and it is produced in ampoules and vials. LSD is a semi-synthetic substance synthesised in 1938 by Hofmann; its effect lasts 8-12 hours.

Let us compare the duration of action. The effect of ketamine lasts 2 hours, and that of psilocin and psilocybin 6 hours. The duration of action of LSD is 8-12 hours; the minimum dose causing hallucinations is 10-25 µg. The maximum blood concentration of phencyclidine appears at 5-15 minutes. Thus, by duration of action, the shortest is ketamine and the longest is LSD.

We compare the mass spectrum peaks. Phencyclidine: 243, 214, 200, 186, 166, 158, 84 and 77 m/z. Ketamine: 180, 209, 182, 152, 181, 30, 211 and 138 m/z. LSD: 44, 72, 207, 221, 280 and 323 m/z. The mass spectra of psilocin and psilocybin include similar peaks: 58, 204, 146, 77 and 44. The table gives all five substances with their m/z values.

On the detection of phencyclidine in urine, according to US data. Phencyclidine appears in urine 4-6 hours after intake and is detected for 7-14 days. The cut-off is 25 ng/ml in both urine screening and confirmation. That is, a result below this value is not considered positive.

To conclude. Phencyclidine was withdrawn from circulation in 1979, ketamine and LSD are hallucinogenic or psychotropic substances; psilocin and psilocybin are DMT derivatives from mushrooms. Preliminary analysis is carried out with Marquis, Mandelin, Ehrlich and Scott reagents; then confirmation is by TLC, GLC, HPLC, UV, IR and GC-MS. For ketamine, the copper sulphate, sodium nitrite-naphthol and Nessler reactions are used; for LSD, the van Urk and Ehrlich reactions.
